thread.title: Dow Drops 130 Points as Alibaba, Microsoft Slip

author: Barron's
title: Dow Drops 130 Points as Alibaba, Microsoft Slip
text:
Stocks look ready to continue their selloff today after a brief respite yesterday .
S&P 500 futures have declined 0.3%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures have fallen 138 points, or 0.5%. Nasdaq Composite futures have dropped 0.6%.
Everyone's looking for someone to blame, whether its a weak productivity reading this morning , the Fed's supposedly hawkish comments that caused the market to shed most of its gain yesterday , the continued slide in the U.S. dollar or concerns about a trade war with China. But Strategas Research Partners Nicholas Bohnsack offers another reason--stocks had just come too far, too fast. "It seems a surprise to no one that the market has taken a few deep breaths this week after its tremendous run over the past 12 months, and in particular following its 8-week melt-up capped a +1.18% move in last Friday's session," he writes. "Time for a break."
But how long will the break last? Bank of America Merrill Lynch technical analyst Stephen Suttmeier notes that the S&P 500 isn't oversold yet, even if it's no longer overbought. He notes that the market is set up for a decline right now, with little support until 2800. "This is a best case scenario with a path to 2900+ if the 2800 area holds," he writes. If it doesn't, a drop to 2770 wouldn't be out of the question.
Look out below?
Getty Images Alibaba Group ( BABA ) has dropped 4% to $196.13 after reporting a profit of $1.63 a share on sales of $12.8 billion. Analysts had predicted earnings of $1.67 a share on sales of $12.4 billion.
eBay ( EBAY ) has soared 10% to $44.81 after reporting an adjusted profit of 59 cents a share on sales of $2.61 billion, while analysts had forecast earnings of 52 cents a share on sales of $3.63 billion, and suggesting it would start diversifying its payments business away from PayPal Holdings ( PYPL ). As a result, PayPal has slumped 7.1% to $79.20. PayPal also reported revenue of $2.61 billion and earnings of 59 cents a share, in line with analyst forecasts. "We urge investors to take advantage of a likely sell-off in PYPL shares tied to concerns over the altered long-term relationship with eBay," Cowen's George Mihalos wrote in a note this morning.
Facebook ( FB ) has risen 2.1% to $190.77 after reporting an adjusted profit of $2.21 on revenue of $12.97 billion. Wall Street had been expecting earnings of $1.95 a share on sales of $12.55 billion. "While News Feed changes have had an impact on engagement in 4Q (~5%), this did not appear to have any material impact on revenue growth," writes Raymond James analyst Aaron Kessler.
Hershey ( HSY ) has dropped 3.9% to $106.00 after reporting a profit of $1.03 a share , below the Street consensus for $1.07, on sales of $1.94 billion, below expectations for $1.96 billion. Hershey also said organic sales in 2018 would be "slighly up to +2% yr/yr" when analysts had been predicting 2%. "As bulls were largely looking for commodity-driven gross margin upside and cost savings-driven SG&A benefits in FY18, the guide implies no net input cost tailwinds and much larger than expected reinvestment," writes Wells Fargo's John Baumgartner.
Mastercard (MA) has risen 2.4% to $173.00 after reporting a profit of $1.14 a share on sales of $3.31 billion. Analysts had predicted $1.12 a share on sales of $3.26 billion.
Microsoft (MSFT) has fallen 1.1% to $93.95 after reporting an adjusted profit of 96 cents a share , beating forecasts for 86 cents a share, on sales of $28.9 billion, ahead of estimates for $28.4 billion. "Even with MSFT remaining in'investment mode', expect EPS growth to ramp in 1H CY18 as margins tick up and the tax rate goes lower," writes Evercore ISI analyst Kirk Materne.
Qorvo (QRVO) has surged 12% to $80.57 after reporting earnings of $1.69 a share on sales of $845.7 million. Analysts had been expecting a profit of $1.60 a share on revenue of $845.7 million. Qorvo's guidance was soft, but was countered by positive comments regarding Apple (AAPL).
AT&T (T) has gained 2.8% to $38.50 after reporting a profit of 78 cents a share on sales of $41.68 billion. Analyst had been expecting a profit of 65 cents a share on sales of $41.2 billion. Not everyone was excited, however. "We continue to believe T will struggle to consistently grow revenue and free cash, and investors will have time to assess the impact of the Time Warner (TWX) acquisition later," writes SunTrust Robinson Humphrey analyst Greg Miller.
United Parcel Service (UPS) has slumped 5.2% to $120.69 after reporting a profit of $1.67 a share , beating forecasts for $1.66, on sales of $18.83 billion, better than the $18.19 analysts had predicted. UPS's guidance, however, was on the light side, while the company plans to increase its capital spending. "This step up in capex will raise concerns as the company has not yet convinced the market that investments in productivity and price will get ahead of mix headwinds caused by the shift to B2C," writes Bernstein analyst David Vernon.
Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX) has gained 4.9% to$175 after reporting an adjusted profit of 61 cents a share on sales of $651.6 million. Analysts had been expecting a profit of 53 cents a share on revenue of $592.8 million. Vertex also said it had chosen two cystic fibrosis drugs to test in a triple combination. "We reiterate our BUY rating on what we've characterized as the best growth story in large-cap biotech with revenue and earnings more than tripling over the next 5 years and no biosimilar or generic issues on the horizon," writes Jefferies analyst Michael Yee.
Petroleo Brasileiro (PBR) has gained 2.3% to $13.67 after getting upgrade to Neutral from Sell at Goldman Sachs.
Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG) has dropped 2.1% to $3189 after getting cut to Sell from Neutral at UBS.
Express Scripts (ESRX) has fallen 1.6% to $77.91 after getting downgraded to Underperform from Market Perform at Bernstein.
Nvidia (NVDA) has declined 1.5% to $242.18 after getting removed from the Goldman Sachs Conviction Buy list.
Tobacco stocks can be very controversial. But they also sport attractive yields and returns.
That dichotomy was on display yesterday when Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Brenda Fitzgerald announced her resignation partly owing to a report that she had purchased shares of tobacco, food and drug companies, including Japan Tobacco (2914.Japan), after she had begun running the agency. an agency that just so happens to oversee tobacco companies. That was first reported by Politico , which also reported that Fitzgerald sold the tobacco stock in October.
Getty Images But even for those without conflicts of interest, tobacco stocks can be very controversial, owing to the harmful effects of cigarette smoking and other related products. But some investors buy them anyway thanks to their' dividend payouts and returns.
Altria Group (MO), a large holding company whose subsidiaries include Philip-Morris USA, has returned only 2.4% over the past year amid concerns about declining U.S. cigarette volumes and potential restrictions on nicotine by the Food and Drug Administration. However, the stock yields 3.8%, and the company has regularly raised its quarterly dividend, most recently to 66 cents a share from 61 cents for an 8% rise. And its 10-year annual return of 17.7% easily bests the S&P 500's result of 9.64% over that time, according to FactSet.
Philip Morris International (PM), which separated from Altria nearly a decade ago and focuses on international markets, yields 4%. Its brands include Parliament, Marlboro, Lark and Merit. The company's stock has an annual return of about 12% since it separated from Altria, vs. 10.4% for the S&P 500.
So controversial? Yes. But as long as they pay those hefty dividends, they may not go out of style.
Amazon.com's (AMZN) relentless quest for world domination continues unabated.
Bloomberg News In the past week or so, it's announced plans with Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) to plunge into private health care , and officially opened its cashier-less grocery store of the future, Go, to the public in Seattle. If that isn't daunting enough, a Wall Street Journal report makes the case that Amazon's advertising business poses a major threat to market leaders Alphabet (GOOGL) and Facebook ( FB ).
Next up: Today, Amazon is expected to report fourth-quarter revenue of $59.9 billion on earnings per share of $1.88. Leading the roll call of glory are sales in North America (up 43% to $37.6 billion), internationally (23% to $17.2 billion) and AWS cloud services (45% to $5.1 billion).
The secret to its success? The answer lies in its approach to business and not being afraid of failure or taking bold risks. (It's also more than willing to post big annual losses in the pursuit of gaining market share.) This experimental approach has led to disruption in such diverse fields as e-commerce, entertainment, groceries, voice-activated assistant and smart homes, says Carl Tsukahara, Chief Marketing Officer at Optimizely, a maker of customer-experience customization software that works with 26 of the Fortune 100.
When risk-averse companies have to deploy new experiences, they often do so by guesswork and hope it works, Tsukahara says. By contrast, Amazon's smart, calculated model creates a baseline, and builds a number of experiments around that. It samples and tests permutations, and learns from outcomes, he says.
So is Amazon indestructible? Hardly.
The Seattle-based company's ambitions come with a potential Achilles Heel: In tackling so many diverse markets, it faces competition from every direction. "We believe the aggressive diversification strategy for Amazon is smart, but it does come with inherent risks as going after grocery (Whole Foods) and now likely healthcare/pharmacy in 2018 could cause some speed bumps around margins and near-term execution risks which are something for investors to keep their eye" on, GBH Insights analyst Daniel Ives wrote in a December note. -- Jon Swartz
